summary: This document describes the problem of caller ID impersonation in VoIP systems interworking with the telephone network. Attackers can fake calling numbers for bulk calling schemes or fraud, and it lays out requirements for a way to authenticate the identity of callers.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 7340 explains why a calling telephone number may not reliably identify the caller, especially when a call crosses between VoIP and the traditional telephone network. It lists requirements for a future system to authenticate caller identity without breaking common call paths or exposing unnecessary information.

questions: how to stop caller id spoofing
why does sip identity not work for phone numbers
subtitle: Why calling-party numbers are easy to spoof and what a secure identity solution must support.

tldr.problem: VoIP and telephone-network interworking weakened confidence in calling-party numbers. Earlier SIP identity approaches had difficulty with telephone-number authority, gateways, and intermediaries that alter signaling.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC reviews call paths and previous approaches, then lists requirements for in-band identity that survives intermediaries, credentials based on number delegations, low overhead, and privacy.
tldr.outcome: RFC 7340 is an Informational problem statement and requirements document, not a protocol. It leaves the security analysis of specific solutions to later documents.

today: RFC 7340 is an Informational RFC and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It states a problem and requirements rather than defining a protocol.

sections.title: The Caller Identity Problem
sections.content:
Interworking between Voice over IP (VoIP) and the traditional telephone network reduced the assurance attached to calling-party numbers and Caller ID. Attackers can use fake numbers to impersonate a person, hide who is calling, place bulk calls, attack voicemail, or target organizations with floods of calls.

The RFC notes that some services legitimately present a number different from the caller's device number, such as a doctor's office or call center. A useful solution must therefore verify legitimate authority to use a number without treating every change in displayed number as abuse.
sections.plainLanguage: A number shown to a call recipient may not reliably identify the caller. Some callers also legitimately use an office or company number instead of their own device number.

sections.title: Call Paths and Identity Methods
sections.content:
The RFC distinguishes in-band identity conveyance, which carries origin information in the call-control protocol, from out-of-band identity verification, which checks a telephone number through a separate mechanism. An authority-delegation infrastructure describes how authority over telephone numbers is assigned, ported, and delegated. A canonical telephone-number form lets systems compare the same number consistently.

The use cases cover VoIP-to-VoIP, calls crossing between VoIP and the telephone network in either direction, calls that cross VoIP between two telephone-network endpoints, and telephone-network calls. The RFC assumes the telephone-network part of a call path cannot be altered and highlights gateways and back-to-back user agents as points where signaling may be recreated or changed.
sections.plainLanguage: Identity can travel with call signaling or be checked through a separate connection. Every gateway between VoIP and telephone networks can affect what identity information survives.

sections.title: Limitations of Earlier Approaches
sections.content:
P-Asserted-Identity lets trusted network entities share a caller identity inside a Trust Domain. The RFC describes it as simple and deployed in SIP telephone-replacement systems, but it has no cryptographic validation and depends on transitive trust among network members.

SIP Identity signs selected parts of a SIP request, including the From value and message body. The RFC identifies two barriers: it covers domain names rather than telephone-number authority, and it does not tolerate intermediaries that alter signed request fields or bodies.

VIPR uses a completed telephone-network call to help identify a number and establish an out-of-band connection for future communication. This does not address a first-time robocall, and its public distributed hash table raises privacy and impersonation concerns.
sections.plainLanguage: Earlier methods either trusted a closed network, relied on certificates for domain names, or helped mainly with repeat callers. None addressed all telephone-number and gateway cases described in the RFC.

sections.title: Changes in Number Authority and Privacy
sections.content:
The RFC points to changes that could support new approaches, including smartphones with both telephone and IP connections and national authorities moving number provisioning services online. It says credentials that express authority over numbers could help, while certificate systems should avoid multiple roots or peers claiming authority for the same number.

Some challenges remain difficult. A SIP gateway may not know whether a number received through the telephone network is authentic, and the RFC says that case may prove beyond repair. It also warns that identity attached to calls can enable pervasive monitoring and says the work is not meant to eliminate anonymity.
sections.plainLanguage: Online number-delegation systems could provide information about who may use a telephone number. Identity systems also need to limit unnecessary disclosure of calling data and preserve room for anonymity.

sections.title: Requirements for a Future Solution
sections.content:
A future system must let intermediaries and end systems generate and validate caller identity without human intervention. It must survive calls that pass through the telephone network and back-to-back user agents, and use credentials that build on existing national number delegations rather than assuming one international root.

The solution must allow number portability and legitimate presentation of a number on behalf of another party. It must keep SIP header expansion small to avoid fragmentation when UDP is used, minimize lookups and cryptographic work, and limit what unauthorized parties can learn about who called whom.

The RFC excludes validation of display names and authentication of call responses; it addresses identity for requests. Security considerations for specific designs are left to solution documents.
sections.plainLanguage: A future solution must work through gateways, support existing number assignments, and allow legitimate calls made on behalf of others. It must also keep messages small and limit exposure of calling relationships.

viz.caption: LIMITATIONS OF THREE APPROACHES REVIEWED IN RFC 7340

cells: Trusted SIP entities share an identity
No cryptographic validation; trust is transitive
Does not establish authority for telephone numbers and breaks when fields change
Uses a telephone-network call to support later out-of-band contact
Does not solve first-time robocalls and raises privacy concerns
